mapping.heading: ## On Codex CLI
lines: JBIT was written for Claude Code; this copy is generated for OpenAI Codex CLI. Where the text or the hook's messages use Claude's names, read them this way:

- **Skills.** Invoke a `jbit:<name>` skill by typing `$jbit:<name>` (for example `$jbit:plan`); that is the form Codex recognises. A typed `/jbit:<name>` or `$<name>` isn't an invocation: the model may find the skill from its description, but nothing guarantees it. When a skill says to run another JBIT skill, open that skill's `SKILL.md` and follow it.

- **Agents.** An Agent call is Codex's `spawn_agent`: `task_name` (lowercase letters, digits and underscores) and `message` (the brief) are required. Pass `model` and `reasoning_effort` only as the plan's Models line sets them, and leave out what it doesn't set; the child then inherits the session's. Give a verifier or reviewer `fork_turns: "none"`, so it starts without this session's history and sees only the brief and the code. Wait with `wait_agent`; `send_message`, `followup_task`, `list_agents` and `interrupt_agent` steer it. JBIT's role agents don't ship on Codex: brief a plain `spawn_agent` with the role.

- **No worktree isolation.** `spawn_agent` has no `isolation: "worktree"`. Build leaves one at a time in the main tree, or in parallel only when each builder owns files no other touches; there is no branch to merge back.
- **Questions.** Where a skill says to ask the user (AskUserQuestion on Claude Code), ask in the chat and wait for the reply.

- **Reviews.** `/code-review` and `/security-review` are Claude Code commands. Here, run a fresh `spawn_agent` with `fork_turns: "none"`, briefed with the same lenses (correctness, then security), and triage what it finds.
- **Instructions.** Codex loads `AGENTS.md`, not `CLAUDE.md`. Where a skill reads or writes `CLAUDE.md`, use that file, and read it yourself at the start of a session.

- **Hooks.** JBIT's hooks run only once the user trusts them (at startup or through `/hooks`), and again after every JBIT update. Without trust there is no `## Now` in context, no gates and no carry-on, and nothing says so.
- **Tools.** {tools}. Edits go through `apply_patch`; the guard covers it and the shell alike.

gaps.what: Hooks need trusting after every install and update
gaps.why: Codex runs a plugin's hooks only once the user trusts them, at startup or through `/hooks`, and any change to the hook script voids that trust silently. Until they're trusted again, JBIT has no `## Now` in context, no gates and no carry-on, and nothing says so; `codex exec` skips untrusted hooks without a warning. The trust prompt warns that trusted hooks run outside the sandbox.
A Codex plugin can't register agents (none of the routes the spike tried did), so the package ships none; builders, verifiers and reviewers are plain `spawn_agent` calls briefed with the role.

Codex recognises a skill only as `$jbit:<name>` (for example `$jbit:autopilot`). A typed `/jbit:plan` or `$plan` reaches the model as plain text, which may still find the skill from its description, with no guarantee.

gaps.what: `approve` may be visible to the model
gaps.why: On Claude Code the model can't invoke `approve`. The package sets `allow_implicit_invocation: false` in its `agents/openai.yaml`, which isn't proven live yet. Either way the hook releases a held stage only on the user's own typed approval.

Unproven: a PreToolUse hook that exits 1 lets the call run on Codex, and what Codex does with a hook it kills on its 30-second timeout wasn't tested. The shipped hook refuses by its own 25-second watchdog first, so this bites only if the hook's event loop blocks.

gaps.what: The guard inside `spawn_agent` children, `write_stdin` and MCP tools
gaps.why: Live runs saw PreToolUse fire only for `Bash` and `apply_patch` in the main session; whether it fires for tool calls in a child agent, for input written into a running shell, or for MCP tools is unproven.
Each hook event is a fresh process, so nothing counts repeated turn ends; the hook's own cap on Stop blocks per prompt bounds the loop instead.
Codex has no cap on Stop blocks, so the hook keeps its own per prompt; an unattended run stops quietly when it's reached. Prompt again to carry on.

gaps.what: Lean's count of agents already running
gaps.why: The Claude hook keeps it in memory across events; a command hook has no running process to keep it in.
Same reason: no in-memory agent list between events.

gaps.what: The reopen check after a commit
gaps.why: It runs before the commit lands, since there's no in-memory state carried to the next event.
The hook runs the Claude hook's TypeScript through Node's type stripping; an older Node can't load it, so guarded tool calls are refused.
They are Claude Code built-ins; on Codex the review runs as a fresh `spawn_agent` briefed with the same lenses.
Codex's `spawn_agent` has none, so parallel builders must own separate files or run one at a time.

gaps.what: Compacting the context before autopilot carries on
gaps.why: Codex gives a command hook no context gauge and no compact call; Codex manages its own context.
Codex loads `AGENTS.md`, not `CLAUDE.md`; the skills tell the model to read `CLAUDE.md` itself.
They are the Claude hook's words and name Claude tools (Agent, Edit, Write); each skill's mapping section translates them.
